warmup.q: Researchers loaded a whole order-processing benchmark into the memory of a disk-based database engine, so no transaction ever waited for the disk, and counted the CPU instructions each transaction ran. Where did most of them go?
options: Waiting for the disk anyway, because the engine still reads pages from its files
The real work: reading and updating the rows the transaction touched
Bookkeeping built for disk: finding pages in the buffer pool, latches, locks and log records
Copying data between the kernel and the database's memory
warmup.why: Harizopoulos and colleagues measured Shore, a classic disk-based engine, with all of its data in RAM. About a third of the instructions went to the buffer manager, and roughly 14%, 16% and 12% to latching, locking and logging. About 1/60 of the instructions did the transaction's useful work. No disk reads happened, so the first option can't be it, and with everything in memory there was no copying from the kernel either. An in-memory store is fast mainly because it drops that machinery. This lesson starts there, then opens up Redis as the example.

sections.h: An in-memory store is fast because it skips the disk format, not only the disk
sections.html:
Lesson 1 put a cache in front of a database. Push the idea further: if the whole dataset fits in RAM, the store can live in memory and use the disk only to survive a restart. Would that beat a database that already has every page cached?

It does, by a wide margin, and not for the reason most people guess. In 2008 Harizopoulos, Abadi, Madden and Stonebraker loaded an order-processing benchmark (TPC-C) into the memory of Shore, a classic disk-based engine, so no transaction ever waited for the disk. Then they counted CPU instructions. About a third went to the buffer manager, the code that finds and pins pages (the Storage track's lesson on the buffer pool). About 14% went to latches, 16% to the lock manager and 12% to building log records. Only about 1/60 of the instructions did the transaction's useful work, and stripping the rest made the engine about 20 times faster. So an in-memory store keeps data as ordinary in-memory structures, such as a hash table whose entries point straight at values, and never translates them to and from a page layout. If it uses the disk at all, it appends a log or writes a snapshot on the side (lesson 9), and reads never come from that copy.

Redis is the best-known store built this way, and it answers a problem you already have. Twenty pods of a payment service handle card authorizations. A client retries a payment with the same idempotency key, the retry lands on a different pod, and that pod must answer "have I seen idem:7f3a?" A HashMap in each pod can't, because pod 3's memory is invisible to pod 11. The database can, for the price of a query per check. You want one map that every pod shares, in memory, over the network.

The simplest version is a server holding a HashMap<String, byte[]> behind SET key value and GET key. It breaks as soon as clients change values: two pods counting a card's authorizations both GET 41 and both SET 42 (the worked example loses four increments in five this way). So the server should know the shape of each value and change it itself. A key is a name such as payment:42, and its value has a type: a string, a hash (a small map of fields), a list, a set, a sorted set, and more in lessons 3 and 4. INCR auths:card:7 adds one on the server, HINCRBY payment:43 amount 50 changes one field, and a command that doesn't fit the type fails with WRONGTYPE. Types like these are easy to offer when everything lives in memory, and hard to build on disk pages.

Memory makes Redis fast, and the network decides how fast. On my laptop a GET from the JVM to the Redis container took about 214 microseconds end to end, and Redis spent about half a microsecond of it running the command. That is lesson 1's ladder again: the round trip is the expensive rung.

The licenses changed twice, so know which server you run. Redis was BSD-licensed up to 7.2. In March 2024 Redis Ltd announced that 7.4 and later would ship under the source-available RSALv2 and SSPLv1, and eight days later the Linux Foundation launched Valkey, a BSD fork of Redis 7.2.4 backed by AWS, Google Cloud, Oracle and others. Redis 8.0 added AGPLv3 as a third choice. Today Redis Open Source is at 8.10.3 (the labs pin redis:8.10.3) and Valkey at 9.1.3. Dragonfly, which speaks the same protocol with a different threading design, moved in v2.1 (November 2026) to its own source-available license, free in production up to 100 vCPUs. Everything in this lesson works on Redis and Valkey alike, and this track names the version whenever a command needs Redis 8.

try.title: Start Redis and poke it
steps: From the labs folder, start the server: docker compose -f env/redis.yml up -d.
Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli and type the commands below, one at a time.
Before the last three, predict: what does TYPE say, and what happens when you GET a hash?
Leave the server running for the rest of the lesson. When you are done for the day, stop it and delete its data with docker compose -f env/redis.yml down -v.

code.title: at the redis-cli prompt
code.html:
PING
SET payment:42 approved
GET payment:42
INCR auths:today
INCR auths:today
HSET payment:43 status approved amount 1250 currency EUR
HINCRBY payment:43 amount 50
TYPE payment:43
GET payment:43
INFO server

try.expect: PING answers PONG and GET payment:42 prints "approved". The two INCRs print (integer) 1 and (integer) 2: the key didn't exist, so Redis started from 0. HSET prints (integer) 3 (three new fields) and HINCRBY prints (integer) 1300, computed on the server. TYPE payment:43 says hash, and GET payment:43 fails with (error) WRONGTYPE Operation against a key holding the wrong kind of value. In the INFO server output, find redis_version:8.10.3 and multiplexing_api:epoll: the server asks the Linux kernel's epoll which sockets have data. That is the loop in the next section.

refs.title: Harizopoulos et al., OLTP Through the Looking Glass, and What We Found There (SIGMOD 2008)
Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 4 (keeping everything in memory)

sections.h: One thread runs every command, one after another
sections.html:
Now the server has thousands of clients, each on its own TCP connection, all sending commands at once. How should one server process serve them?

The obvious design is one thread per connection, the way a classic Java servlet container works. Each thread reads its client's command, runs it and writes the reply. It breaks in two places. Ten thousand connections need ten thousand threads, each with its own stack, and the operating system spends its time switching between them. Worse, two threads can now touch the same key at the same moment. INCR auths:card:7 from two threads is the count++ race again (both read 41, both write 42, one update is lost), this time inside the server, so every key needs a lock and every command pays for locking, even when nobody else is near its key.

Redis goes the other way: one thread runs every command. A single thread must never sit waiting on one quiet socket, so it asks the kernel instead, through a system call (a request a program makes to the operating system). On Linux that call is epoll_wait: "here are 10,000 sockets; tell me which ones have bytes ready, and let me sleep until at least one does." Then the thread serves only those. This loop is the event loop, and it repeats four steps:

  1. Ask the kernel which client sockets have bytes waiting. If none do, sleep until one does.
  2. For each ready client, read the bytes and cut them into complete commands.
  3. Run each command against memory, to the end, and put the reply in that client's output buffer.
  4. Before sleeping again, write the queued replies back to the sockets.

Step 3 is the base model for this whole track. Commands from different clients never overlap. While INCR auths:card:7 runs, nothing else can read or write anything. So every single command is atomic: it happens as one step, and no client ever sees it half done. Fifty pods calling INCR on one key never lose an update, and Redis needs no locks to promise that. Nobody else is running.

The price is the same fact seen from the other side. A command that takes 1.5 seconds holds the only thread for 1.5 seconds, and every other client waits, whatever key it wants. On the lab server a GET costs about half a microsecond of that thread's time, so one 1.5-second command costs as much as three million GETs. The usual culprits are commands whose cost grows with the size of a key: KEYS * over the whole keyspace, HGETALL or SMEMBERS on a key with a million entries, DEL of a huge key, and long Lua scripts. A Lua script is a small program that Redis runs as one command (the Transactions track's lesson on serial execution puts them to work); here it is just the easiest way to keep Redis busy.

try.title: Freeze the server with one script
steps: Open two terminals in the labs folder. In terminal 2, type this but don't press Enter yet: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli GET payment:42.
In terminal 1, run the command below. Its Lua script spins on the server's CPU for 3,000 ms. Switch to terminal 2 at once and press Enter. Predict: when does "approved" appear?
Run the script again with 7000 in place of 3000, then the GET. Wait. When the GET gives up, stop the script from terminal 2: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli SCRIPT KILL.

code.title: terminal 1
code.html: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis redis-cli EVAL "local stop = os.clock() + ARGV[1] / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1" 0 3000

try.expect: The GET hangs, and prints "approved" a moment after terminal 1 prints (integer) 1. A different connection and an unrelated key made no difference. With 7000 ms the GET doesn't wait to the end: at the 5-second mark it fails with (error) BUSY Redis is busy running a script. You can only call SCRIPT KILL or SHUTDOWN NOSAVE. Five seconds is the default busy-reply-threshold. From then on Redis pauses the script now and then to answer other clients, but only with that error, so that you can send SCRIPT KILL. It prints OK, and terminal 1 gets (error) ERR Script killed by user with SCRIPT KILL.... The kill works only because the script has not written anything. A script that has written can only be stopped with SHUTDOWN NOSAVE.

video.title: One thread, many clients: the Redis event loop

sections.h: Redis has several threads, and still only one runs commands
sections.html:
If one thread runs everything, two questions follow. Some jobs are slow by nature: writing a snapshot of 2 GB of data to disk, or freeing the memory of a key with ten million members. Who does those without freezing the loop? And the machine has 8 or 16 cores. Is one thread really all Redis uses?

For the slow jobs, Redis hands the work to helpers that never run commands. The redis.conf file that ships with 8.10 calls Redis "mostly single threaded":

  • Background threads, named bio_* for background I/O, close files, push Redis's on-disk log of writes from memory onto the disk with fsync, and free memory for UNLINK and FLUSHALL ASYNC. Deleting a huge key with UNLINK returns at once. Plain DEL frees the memory on the main thread while everyone waits.
  • To save a snapshot of the whole dataset, Redis starts a copy of itself with fork, and that child process writes the file while the parent keeps serving clients (lesson 9).

For the cores, look at where the time goes for a small command. Running a GET takes half a microsecond. Reading the request from the socket, parsing it and writing the reply are system calls into the kernel plus copying, and together they often cost more than the command. So Redis 6 added I/O threads: helpers that do steps 2 and 4 of the loop (read, parse, write) for many connections in parallel, while the main thread still runs every command in step 3. Redis 8.0 shipped a new implementation of them.

I/O threads are off by default: io-threads 1 means the main thread does all the I/O itself. The config file says to enable them only on machines with 4 or more cores, and to leave one core spare: 3 I/O threads on 4 cores, 7 on 8. Redis measured up to 112% more throughput for 8.0 with 8 I/O threads on a multi-core Intel server. That is a vendor benchmark, and the gain depends on the command mix.

What I/O threads can't do is run two commands at once or make one command faster. They help a server that spends its time moving bytes for many small commands over thousands of connections. They do nothing for a slow HGETALL. When someone says "just add threads", first ask which step of the loop is busy.

Other servers draw the line elsewhere. Valkey 8.0 reworked its I/O threads to run alongside the main thread and hand it commands in batches, and its announcement reports up to 1.2 million requests a second on one AWS instance, up from 380,000 (again a vendor figure). Execution is still one thread. Dragonfly splits the keyspace into shards, one per thread, so every core executes commands for its own keys. That buys throughput, and the price is coordination whenever one command touches keys in two shards. Memcached, the older pure cache, runs several worker threads over one shared table guarded by locks, and stores only plain byte values.

try.title: Count the server's threads
steps: List the threads of the running server with the command below. Linux keeps one folder per thread under /proc/1/task, and comm holds the thread's name.

Start a throwaway server with four I/O threads: docker run --rm -d --name sfz-io4 -m 128m redis:8.10.3 redis-server --io-threads 4. List its threads with the same loop, using docker exec sfz-io4 in place of docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis.
Try to change it at run time: docker exec sfz-io4 redis-cli CONFIG SET io-threads 2. Then remove it: docker rm -f sfz-io4.

code.title: terminal
code.html: docker compose -f env/redis.yml exec redis sh -c 'for t in /proc/1/task/*; do cat $t/comm; done'

try.expect: The default server lists six threads: redis-server (the main thread, the only one that runs commands), bio_close_file, bio_aof, bio_lazy_free, and two jemalloc_bg_thd that belong to the memory allocator. The --io-threads 4 server adds io_thd_1, io_thd_2 and io_thd_3; the main thread counts as I/O thread 0. CONFIG SET io-threads 2 fails with can't set immutable config: you pick the I/O thread count when the server starts.

sections.h: Commands travel as RESP, and clients now speak RESP3
sections.html:
A TCP connection carries a stream of bytes with no boundaries in it. If a client sends two commands quickly, the server may receive both in one read, or half of one. So the server needs a rule for where one command ends and the next begins.

The simplest rule is text lines: SET payment:42 approved, then a newline. Redis still accepts that from someone typing into a raw connection. It breaks as soon as a value contains a space or a newline, and values do: a JSON document, a serialized Java object, any bytes at all. Quoting rules would force the server to inspect every byte of every value.

The fix is to send each length first. That is RESP, the Redis serialization protocol. A command is an array of strings, each with its length in bytes in front:

*2\r\n$3\r\nGET\r\n$10\r\npayment:42\r\n

Read it as: an array (*) of 2 elements, a 3-byte string ($3) GET, a 10-byte string payment:42. \r\n is a carriage return and a line feed, the line ending. Because the server knows each length up front, it reads exactly that many bytes and never looks inside them. The first byte of a reply says what kind of reply it is: +OK is a simple string, :42 an integer, $8 an 8-byte string, $-1 no value, -ERR an error.

That version is RESP2, the standard since Redis 2.0. It has one gap: structured replies come back as flat arrays. HGETALL returns status, approved, amount, 1250, and the client has to know to pair them up. RESP3, available since Redis 6.0, adds real maps (%), sets (~), doubles, booleans, a null (_), and push messages that the server sends without being asked, which client-side caching relies on. Every connection starts in RESP2 and switches when the client sends HELLO 3.

Both Java clients in this track send HELLO 3 when they connect. Jedis 8 made that its default, and falls back to RESP2 if the server refuses. You will rarely look at RESP. You need it when a proxy mangles traffic, when a reply type surprises your code, or when you read a packet capture.

try.title: Talk RESP over a plain socket
steps: Run RespDemo (Java) or RespDemoKt (Kotlin) from the labs folder. It opens a plain socket to port 6379, sends commands as raw RESP and prints every byte both ways, with \r\n made visible.
Before you look, predict the reply bytes for INCR auths:today and for INCR payment:42.
Compare HGETALL payment:45 and GET payment:404 before and after HELLO 3. What changed?

code.title: RespDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.net.Socket; import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets; /** Speaks RESP to Redis over a plain socket, with no client library, and prints every byte. */ public class RespDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws IOException { try (Socket socket = new Socket("localhost", 6379)) { OutputStream out = socket.getOutputStream(); InputStream in = socket.getInputStream(); send(out, in, "PING"); send(out, in, "SET", "payment:42", "approved"); send(out, in, "GET", "payment:42"); send(out, in, "GET", "payment:404"); send(out, in, "INCR", "auths:today"); send(out, in, "INCR", "payment:42"); send(out, in, "HSET", "payment:45", "status", "approved", "amount", "1250"); send(out, in, "HGETALL", "payment:45"); send(out, in, "HELLO", "3"); // switch this connection to RESP3 send(out, in, "HGETALL", "payment:45"); send(out, in, "GET", "payment:404"); } } // a command is an array of bulk strings: *<count>, then $<length> and the bytes of each word static void send(OutputStream out, InputStream in, String... words) throws IOException { StringBuilder cmd = new StringBuilder("*" + words.length + "\r\n"); for (String w : words) { cmd.append('$').append(w.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length).append("\r\n").append(w).append("\r\n"); } out.write(cmd.toString().getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)); out.flush(); // good enough for a demo: on loopback a short reply arrives in one read byte[] buf = new byte[8192]; int n = in.read(buf); System.out.println("> " + show(cmd.toString(), 200)); System.out.println("< " + show(new String(buf, 0, n, StandardCharsets.UTF_8), 90)); } static String show(String s, int max) { String visible = s.replace("\r\n", "\\r\\n"); return visible.length() <= max ? visible : visible.substring(0, max) + "... (" + s.length() + " bytes)"; } }

alt.title: RespDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo import java.io.InputStream import java.io.OutputStream import java.net.Socket /** Speaks RESP to Redis over a plain socket, with no client library, and prints every byte. */ fun main() { Socket("localhost", 6379).use { socket -> val out = socket.getOutputStream() val inp = socket.getInputStream() send(out, inp, "PING") send(out, inp, "SET", "payment:42", "approved") send(out, inp, "GET", "payment:42") send(out, inp, "GET", "payment:404") send(out, inp, "INCR", "auths:today") send(out, inp, "INCR", "payment:42") send(out, inp, "HSET", "payment:45", "status", "approved", "amount", "1250") send(out, inp, "HGETALL", "payment:45") send(out, inp, "HELLO", "3") // switch this connection to RESP3 send(out, inp, "HGETALL", "payment:45") send(out, inp, "GET", "payment:404") } } // a command is an array of bulk strings: *<count>, then $<length> and the bytes of each word private fun send(out: OutputStream, inp: InputStream, vararg words: String) { val cmd = buildString { append("*${words.size}\r\n") for (w in words) append("$${w.toByteArray().size}\r\n$w\r\n") } out.write(cmd.toByteArray()) out.flush() // good enough for a demo: on loopback a short reply arrives in one read val buf = ByteArray(8192) val n = inp.read(buf) println("> " + show(cmd, 200)) println("< " + show(String(buf, 0, n), 90)) } private fun show(s: String, max: Int): String { val visible = s.replace("\r\n", "\\r\\n") return if (visible.length <= max) visible else visible.take(max) + "... (${s.length} bytes)" }

try.expect: PING gets +PONG and the first INCR auths:today gets :1 (higher if you ran the first Try it). INCR payment:42 gets -ERR value is not an integer or out of range . Before HELLO 3, HGETALL payment:45 returns a flat array, *4 $6 status ..., and the client has to pair the items up itself. After it, the same command returns a map, %2 ..., holding two field-value pairs. A missing key is $-1 in RESP2 and _ in RESP3. The reply to HELLO 3 is itself a map of about 690 bytes (the exact size depends on your connection id) that starts with the server name, version 8.10.3 and proto 3.

sections.h: This track uses Jedis, and Lettuce where Kotlin needs it
sections.html:
Nobody should format RESP by hand, so you use a client library. The choice that matters inside a client is how the threads of your service share TCP connections.

The first design is a pool. The client keeps several open connections. A call borrows one, sends one command, waits for the reply and gives the connection back. While one thread waits, others use other connections. Every call blocks its thread for one round trip, and threads queue when all connections are busy: Jedis's pool holds at most 8 connections unless you configure more, so 200 request threads on 8 connections take turns. This is Jedis.

The second design is multiplexing: one connection shared by every thread. Calls write their commands onto the same socket back to back, without waiting for each other. Redis answers the commands on a connection in the order they arrived, so the client keeps a queue of callers and hands each reply to the next caller in line. One connection carries thousands of calls in flight. The cost is that your code gets a future, a callback or a suspended coroutine instead of a plain value. This is Lettuce.

Jedis 8.0.2 gives you one RedisClient, built with RedisClient.builder(), with the pool behind it. Lettuce 7.9.0, built on Netty, has a sync API, an async API that returns RedisFuture (a CompletionStage), a reactive API on Project Reactor, and a Kotlin coroutines API. The coroutines API is a layer over the reactive one, so it needs both kotlinx-coroutines-core and kotlinx-coroutines-reactive on the classpath, and an opt-in annotation, @ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi.

This track teaches with Jedis. One call is one command and one reply, so your code maps line for line onto what you type in redis-cli, and the lessons stay about Redis instead of about futures. Lettuce shows up where it changes the picture: Kotlin coroutines, and many calls sharing one connection. If your Quarkus services use the Quarkus Redis extension, that one is built on the Vert.x Redis client and works like Lettuce: non-blocking, few connections.

One trap: both libraries name their entry class RedisClient. In a file that uses both, write one of them with its full package name.

Java
RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build();
redis.set("payment:42", "approved");
String status = redis.get("payment:42");          // blocks until the reply arrives
Kotlin
val redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()
redis.set("payment:42", "approved")
val status: String? = redis.get("payment:42")     // GET of a missing key returns null

try.title: Ask the server who connected
steps: Run ClientsDemo (Jedis and Lettuce's async API) or ClientsDemoKt (Jedis and Lettuce's coroutines). Each does the same GET through both libraries, then asks the server for its list of connections.
Read the last two lines. They are the server's own view of each connection, from CLIENT LIST.

code.title: ClientsDemo.java
code.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo; import io.lettuce.core.RedisFuture; import io.lettuce.core.api.StatefulRedisConnection; import io.lettuce.core.api.async.RedisAsyncCommands; import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.regex.Matcher; import java.util.regex.Pattern; /** The same GET through Jedis (blocking) and Lettuce (async), then how each one connected. */ public class ClientsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { // Jedis 8: one RedisClient, a pool of connections behind it, blocking calls try (RedisClient jedis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build()) { jedis.set("payment:42", "approved"); System.out.println("Jedis GET payment:42 -> " + jedis.get("payment:42")); // Lettuce 7: one connection shared by every caller, calls return futures io.lettuce.core.RedisClient lettuce = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379"); try (StatefulRedisConnection<String, String> conn = lettuce.connect()) { RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> async = conn.async(); RedisFuture<String> reply = async.get("payment:42"); // returns at once System.out.println("Lettuce GET payment:42 -> " + reply.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); // ask the server how each library connected String list = async.clientList().get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS); Pattern fields = Pattern.compile("(resp=\\d+) (lib-name=\\S+) (lib-ver=\\S+)"); for (String line : list.split("\n")) { Matcher m = fields.matcher(line); if (m.find() && !m.group(2).equals("lib-name=")) { System.out.println(m.group(1) + " " + m.group(2) + " " + m.group(3)); } } } finally { lettuce.shutdown(); } } } }

alt.title: ClientsDemo.kt
alt.html: package sfz.cache.l02.demo import io.lettuce.core.ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi import io.lettuce.core.api.coroutines import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import redis.clients.jedis.RedisClient /** The same GET through Jedis (blocking) and Lettuce (coroutines), then how each one connected. */ @OptIn(ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi::class) fun main() { // Jedis 8: one RedisClient, a pool of connections behind it, blocking calls RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build().use { jedis -> jedis.set("payment:42", "approved") println("Jedis GET payment:42 -> " + jedis.get("payment:42")) // Lettuce 7: one connection shared by every caller; coroutines suspend instead of blocking val lettuce = io.lettuce.core.RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379") try { lettuce.connect().use { conn -> val redis = conn.coroutines() val list = runBlocking { println("Lettuce GET payment:42 -> " + redis.get("payment:42")) // suspends redis.clientList().orEmpty() // ask the server how each library connected } val fields = Regex("""(resp=\d+) (lib-name=\S+) (lib-ver=\S+)""") list.lineSequence() .mapNotNull { fields.find(it) } .filter { it.groupValues[2] != "lib-name=" } .forEach { println(it.groupValues.drop(1).joinToString(" ")) } } } finally { lettuce.shutdown() } } }

try.expect: Both versions print approved twice, then resp=3 lib-name=jedis lib-ver=8.0.2 and resp=3 lib-name=Lettuce lib-ver=7.9.0.RELEASE/1d7b2b2. Both libraries switched to RESP3 with HELLO 3, and both told the server who they are with CLIENT SETINFO. On a shared production Redis, CLIENT LIST therefore shows which library and version every connection uses.

refs.title: Jedis v7 to v8 migration guide

analogy: A Redis server is a bank branch with one very fast teller and many doors. Customers queue at their own door. The teller takes the request at the front of each door in turn, finishes it completely, puts the receipt in that door's tray and moves on. No two requests are ever half-done at the same time, so the ledger stays consistent without anyone locking anything. But a customer who asks the teller to count a sack of coins holds up every door. I/O threads are assistants who carry requests to the counter and receipts back, but only the teller touches the ledger. The analogy breaks on speed: a real teller needs a minute per customer, while Redis needs about half a microsecond, so queues that would be hopeless in a bank stay invisible in Redis until one slow request arrives.
world: Your payment service probably already uses Redis for idempotency keys, rate limits or a cache of card-issuer responses. All of them share one execution thread with every other service on that Redis. When the fraud team's nightly job runs KEYS fraud:* on the shared instance, your authorization path's GET idem:... calls wait behind it, and your p99 jumps from 1 ms to however long that command takes. Nothing in your service changed, and the Redis host's CPU graph looks calm: one core is busy and the rest are idle. Two habits follow. Treat every command on a big key as a cost that every client pays. And when Redis latency spikes for all keys at once, look for one slow command first (SLOWLOG GET), before you look at the network or ask for more threads.
mistake: The most common mistake is reading "single-threaded" as "slow" or "can't use more cores", and then fixing the wrong thing. Teams turn on io-threads or buy a bigger instance when the real problem is one O(N) command, one whose cost grows with the size of a key: a KEYS *, an HGETALL on a hash that grew to a million fields, a DEL of a huge set, a Lua script that loops over thousands of keys. More cores can't help, because only one thread executes commands. Find the command instead: SLOWLOG GET lists every command that took longer than 10 ms (the default slowlog-log-slower-than is 10000 microseconds). Then replace it with an incremental one: SCAN for KEYS, HSCAN for HGETALL, UNLINK for DEL, and several smaller keys for one giant key.

compare.title: Lettuce from Java and from Kotlin: one connection, two styles

java.title: PaymentStatus.java
java.html: // Lettuce async: every call returns a RedisFuture at once RedisClient client = RedisClient.create("redis://localhost:6379"); try (StatefulRedisConnection<String, String> conn = client.connect()) { RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> redis = conn.async(); RedisFuture<String> status = redis.get("payment:42"); RedisFuture<Long> auths = redis.incr("auths:today"); // both commands are already on the wire; now wait for the replies System.out.println(status.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS) + " " + auths.get(1, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } finally { client.shutdown(); }

kotlin.title: PaymentStatus.kt
kotlin.html: // Lettuce coroutines: calls suspend instead of returning futures @OptIn(ExperimentalLettuceCoroutinesApi::class) suspend fun printStatus(client: RedisClient) { client.connect().use { conn -> val redis = conn.coroutines() coroutineScope { val status = async { redis.get("payment:42") } val auths = async { redis.incr("auths:today") } println("${status.await()} ${auths.await()}") } } }

compare.note: Both versions put two commands on one connection before waiting for either reply, so the INCR doesn't wait a round trip for the GET. Java gets that with futures. Kotlin gets it with async and await, and the code reads top to bottom. The coroutines API is a layer over Lettuce's reactive API, which is why it needs kotlinx-coroutines-reactive on the classpath and an opt-in annotation. Jedis code looks the same in both languages: it blocks, so there is nothing to translate.

worked.title: Count authorizations from eight threads without losing any

steps.say: A settlement job counts today's authorizations in Redis. Eight worker threads share one Jedis RedisClient, and each one reads the counter, adds 1 and writes it back. Predict what it prints after 8,000 calls.
steps.code: RedisClient redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build(); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8); for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) { pool.submit(() -> { String v = redis.get("auths:today"); // 1. read long n = v == null ? 0 : Long.parseLong(v); // 2. add redis.set("auths:today", String.valueOf(n + 1)); // 3. write }); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES); System.out.println(redis.get("auths:today"));

alt.html: val redis = RedisClient.builder().hostAndPort("localhost", 6379).build() val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(8) repeat(8_000) { pool.submit { val v: String? = redis.get("auths:today") // 1. read val n = v?.toLong() ?: 0L // 2. add redis.set("auths:today", (n + 1).toString()) // 3. write } } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(1, TimeUnit.MINUTES) println(redis.get("auths:today"))

steps.say: Three runs against the lab server printed 1,611, then 1,654, then 1,628. About four in five increments vanished. Each command was atomic, but the pair was not. Between one thread's GET and its SET, the event loop ran other threads' commands, so several threads read the same old value and wrote the same new one. It is count++ again, with a network round trip widening the gap.

Let the server do the read, the add and the write as one command. INCR runs to completion inside the loop, so nothing can come between its read and its write. The same job now prints 8000 on every run.
steps.code: for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) { pool.submit(() -> redis.incr("auths:today")); // one command: read, add and write on the server }

alt.html: repeat(8_000) { pool.submit { redis.incr("auths:today") } // one command: read, add and write on the server }

steps.say: With Lettuce, Kotlin can send all 8,000 INCRs from coroutines over a single connection, with no thread pool at all. Each incr suspends until its reply arrives, and the commands queue up on the one socket. On the lab server this took about 230 ms (it depends on your machine and Docker) and printed 8000. The Java twin uses the async API and waits with CompletableFuture.allOf.
steps.code: val redis = conn.coroutines() coroutineScope { repeat(8_000) { launch { redis.incr("auths:today") } } // 8,000 coroutines, one connection } println(redis.get("auths:today")) // 8000

alt.html: RedisAsyncCommands<String, String> redis = conn.async(); List<CompletableFuture<Long>> calls = new ArrayList<>(); for (int i = 0; i < 8_000; i++) calls.add(redis.incr("auths:today").toCompletableFuture()); CompletableFuture.allOf(calls.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0])).join(); System.out.println(redis.get("auths:today").get()); // 8000

lab.title: Model the event loop, then catch the real one blocking
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All eight fail: five in EventLoopTest, a model that needs no Docker, and three in SlowScriptProbeTest, which run against a real Redis 8.10 container that Testcontainers starts for you.
Write EventLoop.runUntilIdle() in EventLoop.kt. The KDoc lists the four steps. Take the snapshot of arrived commands once per pass, before you run any of them.

Run ./gradlew :redis:test --tests 'sfz.cache.l02.EventLoopTest' until its five tests pass. Read the test a command that arrives during a pass waits for the next pass: the real loop behaves the same way.

Write timeGet and timeGetDuringScript in SlowScriptProbe.java. Start the script on the scripts client in a background thread, sleep HEAD_START_MS, time the GET on the app client, then wait for the script.
Run all eight tests. The Docker tests take a few seconds, because they block the server on purpose.
hints: pending.filter { it.arrivedAt <= clock } gives you the snapshot. Loop over clients, and inside that over the snapshot entries of that client, so each client's commands keep their order.
If nothing has arrived, set clock = pending.minOf { it.arrivedAt } and go round again. Without that, an idle loop spins forever and the test times out.

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> scripts.eval(BUSY_SCRIPT, 0, String.valueOf(scriptMillis))) runs the script in the background. Call join() on it before you return, so a script error fails the call.

drill.title: Write the slow-script probe from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. In a blank file, write timeGetDuringScript(scripts, app, key, millis): start a busy Lua script on one client in the background, wait 200 ms, time a GET on the other client, wait for the script, and return the GET's milliseconds. Write the Lua too. Then compare with the answer. Did you remember why the script needs its own thread?

answer.html: static final String BUSY = "local stop = os.clock() + tonumber(ARGV[1]) / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1"; static long timeGetDuringScript(RedisClient scripts, RedisClient app, String key, long millis) throws InterruptedException { CompletableFuture<Object> script = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync( () -> scripts.eval(BUSY, 0, String.valueOf(millis))); // eval blocks a pool thread, not us Thread.sleep(200); // head start: the script is running long t0 = System.nanoTime(); app.get(key); // waits for the script to end long ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000; script.join(); return ms; }

alt.html: const val BUSY = "local stop = os.clock() + tonumber(ARGV[1]) / 1000 while os.clock() < stop do end return 1" fun timeGetDuringScript(scripts: RedisClient, app: RedisClient, key: String, millis: Long): Long { val script = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { scripts.eval(BUSY, 0, millis.toString()) } // eval blocks a pool thread Thread.sleep(200) // head start: the script is running val t0 = System.nanoTime() app.get(key) // waits for the script to end val ms = (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000 script.join() return ms }

recap: An in-memory store is fast mainly because it keeps data in plain memory structures, without the buffer pool, latches, locks and log records a disk-based engine runs even when every page is cached.
Redis keeps typed data structures in memory, and commands change them on the server, so you rarely read, modify and write back.

One thread runs every command, one after another, each to completion. That makes every single command atomic without any locks, and lets one slow command (KEYS *, HGETALL on a huge hash, a long Lua script) stall every client.

Background threads, a forked child and optional I/O threads (io-threads, off by default) do side work and never execute commands. Valkey shares that model; Dragonfly runs one execution thread per shard.
Clients speak RESP, and Jedis 8 and Lettuce 7.9 switch to RESP3 with HELLO 3. This track teaches with Jedis's blocking RedisClient, and uses Lettuce for Kotlin coroutines.
Redis is RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3 from 8.0 (8.10.3 now); Valkey (9.1.3) is the BSD fork; Dragonfly moved to a source-available license in v2.1.

explain.prompt: A teammate says: "Redis is single-threaded, so it can't keep up with us. Let's turn on I/O threads so it runs our commands in parallel." Explain what is right and what is wrong in that, in your own words.
explain.answer: Redis does execute commands on one thread, one at a time, each to completion. That is why each command is atomic, and why one slow command makes everyone wait. But one thread is rarely the limit for small commands: a GET costs about half a microsecond. I/O threads don't run commands in parallel. They take over reading sockets, parsing commands and writing replies, which helps when the server spends its time on network bytes for many connections. If our problem is latency spikes, the likely cause is one slow O(N) command, and I/O threads won't touch it. I'd check SLOWLOG GET first and replace the slow command with an incremental one.

deeper.html:
The 2008 measurement is worth reading in full. With its data cached and logging on, Shore ran about 640 New Order transactions a second. The authors then removed one piece at a time: logging, locking, latching, then the buffer manager. The fully stripped engine ran about 12,700 a second on one thread, about 20 times faster, and a hand-written kernel doing only the useful work about 46,500. No single piece dominated, which is why tuning one of them in a disk-based engine never closes the gap. The H-Store research system, and VoltDB after it, came from the same group of people and the same argument: partition the data, run each partition's transactions one at a time on one thread, and keep everything in memory. Designing Data-Intensive Applications, 2nd edition, chapter 4, makes the same point about in-memory databases and cites this paper.

Why is one thread fast enough? Most commands touch one key and finish in well under a microsecond, the data is already in RAM, and with no second thread there are no locks to take and no cache lines bouncing between cores. For small commands the expensive part is usually the system calls: one read and one write per command per client. That is the cost pipelining attacks (send many commands, read many replies, pay the syscalls once; the Transactions track's lesson on serial execution uses it) and I/O threads spread over cores.

The real loop is a little richer than the lab's model. When a client has sent several commands at once, Redis reads a buffer's worth of bytes and runs every complete command in it before moving to the next client. That is why a pipelined batch from one client runs back to back, and why a client that sends a huge batch can delay the clients after it in the same pass.

One thing surprised me while writing this lesson. The first busy script I tried looped on redis.call('TIME') until 2,000 ms had passed. It ran for 5 seconds instead. Inside a script, TIME kept returning the moment the script started, and it only moved when the 5-second busy handling kicked in. os.clock() measures CPU time, which keeps moving, so the lab uses it. If you ever write a script that waits on server time, it won't work for the same reason, and you shouldn't want a script that waits anyway.

If you want the source, src/ae.c in the Redis repository is the event loop library (it wraps epoll on Linux and kqueue on macOS), and src/networking.c reads queries and writes replies.
